about: Five of the eleven texts, changed after your first read. Same task as before.

texts.heading: It always goes deeper
texts.problem_fixed: Model one-line summary: "is not the same question as what makes me loved"; "in that particular way" vague.
sentences: Some women are fixer types, which can create the opposite pattern.
Before me, Bee had housed and supported a boyfriend who was totally broke and crazy, for a while.
Later she blamed herself for staying through that, and I agree, it wasn't appropriate.
It's not the same as helping carry somebody through a temporary incapacity, like she did with my knee.
What I still want to know is whether she’ll love me through a stretch when I can’t provide, like with my knee.

texts.heading: Slow & steady isn’t KO’d yet
texts.problem_fixed: Model recap: four clipped lines restate B191; "Sex itself tells you other things" vague.
sentences: Women are always demanding to know why I love them.
Apparently they’re allowed not to know.
Those double-standards really bug me, but I also understand our brains work differently.
So that’s another thing to learn about over time in a relationship, and it sometimes hits you unexpectedly.
Go slowly if you can, then, and learn what you can about each other before sex, but there are things you’ll only find out once you’re having it, like how your bodies respond to each other.

texts.heading: Attraction and exclusivity
texts.problem_fixed: Stumble: "this ironically bureaucratic basis of romance" unclear; bonobo sentence doesn't connect to the first.
sentences: Ironically, sexclusivity, which we treat as the basis of romance, started out as that kind of bureaucratic record-keeping.
By the 17th century, when England began mass urbanization by forcing peasants off their land, it had become the legal definition of marriage.

As for what comes naturally to us underneath that law, I’m not trying to say we’re just like bonobos, but the academic consensus is that humans tend toward flexible pair-bonding, with a propensity for occasional infidelity.

texts.heading: What will honesty produce?
texts.problem_fixed: Stumble: "If the other person won’t look" doesn't follow the Bee story; "It is its own reward" cliché.
sentences: Many people ask this question of honesty, but it’s unfair, because honesty is worth having whatever it leads to, and it can lead to very different places.
It might repair the relationship, make it an open one, turn the romance into friendship, preserve the family through separation, or show you that ending it is better.
With Bee and me, it led to a temporary separation, which helped us, and that separation then became more permanent, although I’ve always thought maybe we would get back together in a few decades.
Any of those outcomes takes both of you, though, so if the other person won’t look at the truth with you, you can’t make it mutual, and then you have to decide what you can live with.

texts.heading: What I gained from loss
texts.problem_fixed: Model: one point said three times ("only by the result", "process of growth", "not only whether you stayed").
sentences: From H., I learned that I can be extremely close to someone and feel completely understood and supported without actually falling in love.
I still treasure the support we gave/give each other.
Too many people judge a relationship only by whether they stayed together.
Relationships are a process of growth in many dimensions, so start measuring what you actually learned from yours.
